# Query-Driven Visualization


## Overview
Query-Driven Visualization (QDV) integrates database technologies with visualization strategies to address the increasing size and complexity of scientific datasets [S1, unofficial]. It uses user-specified selection queries to identify spatial regions of interest, reducing the data subset for efficient analysis and visualization [S1, unofficial]. Unlike siblings that focus on hardware acceleration or spatial partitioning for rendering performance, QDV focuses on semantic data reduction, allowing users to extract meaningful subsets (e.g., combustion fronts, pollution areas) based on domain-specific criteria before rendering [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
This family shares the core mechanisms of [Out-of-core, streaming and distributed data](8-out-of-core-streaming-and-distributed-data.md). QDV specifically relies on the **Decomposition Strategy** to partition data into manageable subdomains that can be queried [S1, unofficial]. It utilizes **Work Assignment** to process only the data subsets identified by the queries, thereby minimizing $T_{compute}$ for the relevant regions [S1, unofficial]. While **Compositing Order** remains critical for correct alpha blending, QDV often operates on smaller, disjoint subsets of the volume, potentially simplifying the compositing tree if the query results are spatially coherent [S1, unofficial]. **Communication Overhead** is reduced because the query engine filters data at the source or storage layer before it is transferred to the visualization pipeline [S1, unofficial]. **Caching and Prefetching** strategies are applied to the query results and the underlying data blocks required to evaluate the selection criteria [S1, unofficial].

Not given in the sources.

## Background
Query-Driven Visualization was first presented by Stockinger et al., who demonstrated the coupling of visualization with high-performance query technology [S1, unofficial]. The technique was developed to handle the continually increasing size and complexity of scientific datasets [S1, unofficial]. It is used in the DEX software system by Stockinger et al. [S1, unofficial]. In this context, QDV is applied to extract function field features, such as golf courses, water, and pollution areas, from hyperspectral and air quality simulation data [S1, unofficial]. Features are defined as spatial regions where 1-dimensional functions are similar, specified as Boolean range queries over closed intervals [S1, unofficial].
